Appendix A Experimental Details and Additional Results

A.1 Numerical comparisons

We directly compare the numerical performance of the methods that we have presented in a synthetic first-order autoregressive (AR) process. An AR process is a sequence of random variables where the elements in the sequence depend on the previous value plus a noise term. Although the elements in the sequence are correlated, the mean of the process can be designed to have any shape. Loosely, we model the loss of example i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,...,n\} as an independently drawn AR process indexed by a one dimensional ordered set of Λ\Lambda, with a “V”-shaped mean. In other words, the risk is “V”-shaped, with the tip falling below α\alpha. We will make this description mathematically concrete in a moment.

In addition to the multiple testing strategies presented in the main text, we consider an alternative approach outlined in Appendix E, using uniform concentration results to guarantee risk control. Unfortunately, this approach was seen to be more conservative than the multiple testing approach in the main-text examples.

Now, we turn to the concrete definition of our AR process. We consider a case where Λ={0.001,0.002,…,1}\Lambda=\{0.001,0.002,\dots,1\} and the true risk R⁡(λ)R(\lambda) is “V”-shaped, falling below the desired level α\alpha in the center of the interval; see Figure 11. For each observation i=1,…,ni=1,\dots,n, we simulate losses for 𝒯λj\mathcal{T}_{\lambda_{j}} from the following first-order autoregressive model:

Li,j\displaystyle L_{i,j} =Φ⁡(uj+μj)\displaystyle=\Phi(u_{j}+\mu_{j}) (37)
uj\displaystyle u_{j} =corr⋅uj−1+1−corr2⋅𝒩⁡(0,1).\displaystyle=\mathrm{corr}\cdot u_{j-1}+\sqrt{1-\mathrm{corr}^{2}}\cdot\mathcal{N}(0,1). (38)

Here, the μj\mu_{j} are chosen in such a way as to create the “V”-shaped risk curve; note that there is no dependence on ii anywhere, because an independent random process gets generated for each sample i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,...,n\}. From this simulated data, we form p-values for each hypothesis in (3) using the Hoeffding-Bentkus bound from Section 2.3. Then, we apply the Bonferroni test and the fixed sequence test to these p-values.

Before turning to the results, we pause to think about the meaning of our setting. Here, we wish to find a value of λ\lambda such that the risk is below α\alpha, but do not know in advance where this may happen. Therefore, we use the data to test whether the risk is below α\alpha for each value of λ\lambda using the calibration data. Note that because in practice all tests are based on the same calibration data, the results will be dependent, which is why our simulated setting includes the autoregressive correlation term.

The results are recorded in Figure 11, which we parse next. Firstly, the uniform concentration bound, perhaps predictably, performs badly in practice; see our discussion of this topic in Section 8. Secondly, the fixed sequence method is less conservative than the Bonferroni method, as expected; fixed sequence testing is designed to make the rejection set as wide as possible on the right side.

A.2 Additional experimental results for FDR control

In Figure 12, we report additional results from the experiment from Section 3, this time with desired FDR level α=0.5\alpha=0.5.

A.3 Details about the ODIN score

Next, we precisely define the ODIN function, which we use for as an OOD score. Let f^y​(x)\hat{f}_{y}(x) be the output of the DenseNet’s final, temperature-scaled [70] softmax layer, meant to estimate ℙ⁡(Y∣X)\mathbb{P}\left(Y\mid X\right). Additionally, let f^(i)​(x)\hat{f}_{(i)}(x) be the softmax output of the ii-th most likely class. The key step in ODIN is to add a small perturbation to the input image designed to help distinguish between in-distribution and out-of-distribution images. In particular, the perturbation

w⁡(X)=X−ϵ​sign​(−∇X​log​f^(1)​(X))w(X)=X-\epsilon\,\mathrm{sign}\left(-\nabla_{X}\log\hat{f}_{(1)}(X)\right) (39)

encourages the top softmax output to be more confident on the perturbed input w⁡(X)w(X). The tuning parameter ϵ\epsilon is the magnitude of the perturbation—we took it to be 0.0014, the default value from the ODIN GitHub repository. Then, the OOD function is taken to be

OOD⁡(X)=1−f^​(w⁡(X))(1).\mathrm{OOD}(X)=1-\hat{f}(w(X))_{(1)}. (40)

The reader can view ODIN as an improvement upon the obvious OOD function, 1−f^​(X)(1)1-\hat{f}(X)_{(1)}; the improvement relies on the empirical observation that the top softmax output grows more for in-distribution images when perturbed than it does for out-of-distribution images.

We make one final note here about the scaling of the ODIN function. With this particular model on the CIFAR-10 dataset, all values of OOD⁡(X)\mathrm{OOD}(X) were between the numbers 0.8900.890 and 0.8990.899. In other words, this score is extremely poorly scaled; when choosing 1000 equally spaced points between 0 and 1000, only 9 of them will land in this interval. We re-scaled ODIN manually to fix this problem, although it could be fixed using the training dataset.

Appendix B Proofs

Proof of Theorem 1.

The result is immediate. ∎

Proof of Proposition 1.

This is a combination of the results from [46] and [47]. See [2] for details on how to hybridize the two inequalities. ∎

Proof of Proposition 2.

This is a straightforward consequence of the central limit theorem. A statement can be found in any graduate probability textbook, such as [71]. ∎

Proof of Proposition 3.

This is a classical result in multiple testing. For example, see [45] for discussion. ∎

Proof of Proposition 4.

Fixed sequence testing has existed in the literature for some time; see, e.g., [49] and [44]. We include a proof of the version we use for completeness.

Consider first the case where |𝒥||\mathcal{J}| = 1. Then there will be a first index at which you encounter a null. The probability of making a false discovery at that index is bounded by δ\delta. Thus, the probability of making any false discoveries is bounded by δ\delta.

Turning to the |𝒥|>1|\mathcal{J}|>1 case, the procedure is equivalent to running many instances of the |𝒥|=1|\mathcal{J}|=1 procedure in parallel, at level δ/|𝒥|\delta/|\mathcal{J}|. By the union bound, the probability of any false rejections is then bounded by δ\delta. ∎

Proof of Proposition 5.

Since the procedure is sequential, it rejects a null iff it rejects Hj∗H_{j^{*}}, in which case pj∗≤δp_{j^{*}}\leq\delta. ∎

Proof of Proposition 7.

The result is immediate. ∎

Proof of Proposition 8.

By the definition of a uniform bound, R+R^{+} fails with probability at most α\alpha at λ^\hat{\lambda}. ∎

Appendix C Split Fixed Sequence Testing

In Section 2.3.4, we showed how any pre-specified SGT can control the FWER. The technique is flexible and powerful, especially for situations where it is straighforward to hand-design a graph, such as Figure 6 in the OOD detection example. However, for the large-scale machine learning systems we use, designing the graph is not always scaleable. For example, consider the object detection example in Section 7. Because all three coordinates of λ\lambda affect all three risks, and we do not know a-priori which values of λ\lambda control the risks, there is no graph that is obviously best. In such situations, we might desire an automated procedure that defines the graph by looking at promising hypotheses in our data; in other words, we seek to learn the graph.

The procedure we define here, which we call split fixed sequence testing, is a very simple way of learning the graph from an extra data split. The idea is inspired by the following fact: in many settings, we hope to identify points that violate several risk functions equally often. Therefore, we pick a sequence of λ\lambda that have nearly the same p-value using the first split of data. Then, we simply use fixed sequence testing on this selected sequence using the fresh data. This allows us to decide our path through Λ\Lambda using data while still providing rigorous FWER control.

Concretely, the algorithm begins by partitioning the calibration data points ℐcal\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{cal}} into a graph selection set ℐgraph\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{graph}} and a multiple testing set ℐtesting\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{testing}}. We will learn our path through Λ\Lambda only by looking at ℐgraph\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{graph}}; we will reserve the other split of data simply for running SGT. Following the notation from Section 2.4, and calculating the p-values only on the graph selection set ℐgraph\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{graph}}, we define the function

λ~​(β)=λj​, where ​j=arg⁡minj′​‖[pj,1,…,pj,m]−[β,…,β]‖∞,\tilde{\lambda}(\beta)=\lambda_{j}\text{, where }j=\underset{j^{\prime}}{\arg\min}\Big|\Big|[p_{j,1},...,p_{j,m}]-[\beta,...,\beta]\Big|\Big|_{\infty}, (41)

where β\beta ranges from 00 to 11. The function λ~​(β)\tilde{\lambda}(\beta) picks a point where the p-values for all risks are nearly equal to β\beta. We parameterize our path by discretizing this function. For some positive integer DD, we set

λ~d=λ~​(dD)​, for ​d=0,1,…,D.\tilde{\lambda}_{d}=\tilde{\lambda}\left(\frac{d}{D}\right)\text{, for }d=0,1,...,D. (42)

Note that in practice, this sequence can have repeated values, usually adjacent to one another; we remove them in practice, and ignore them for notational convenience.

Once we have the sequence {λ~d}d=0D\{\tilde{\lambda}_{d}\}_{d=0}^{D}, we do fixed sequence testing directly on the sequence as it is naturally ordered using the multiple testing set ℐtesting\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{testing}}. Figure 10 shows the result of this procedure in our object detection example.

Appendix D Hamming-equalized SGT

Recall that the SGT procedure from Section 2.3 allows us to design any graph to propagate our error budget while still controlling type-I error. We considered two hand-designed graphs in the main text: the fallback procedure and the so-called Hamming graph presented in Figure 6. Now, we return to the Hamming graph, which improves upon the fallback procedure under certain conditions, and discuss its properties here. In the Hamming graph, all of the error budget starts in the bottom-right corner, and propagates through two subparts of the graph. In the lower-right triangle, the graph perfuses the error budget such that nodes with equal Hamming distance from the bottom-right node are designed to receive the same error budget if all previous nodes reject. We will call this property balanced inflow; see Definition 3 below. In the upper-left triangle, the graph propagates the error leftwards.

Concretely, we associate the index (i,j)(i,j) to the node in the iith row from the bottom and the jjth row from the right of the graph. Then we set the weights of our graph to

W(i,j)→(i,j+1)={ji+ji+j≤N1i+j>N​ and ​i=N0 else,W_{(i,j)\to(i,j+1)}=\begin{cases}\frac{j}{i+j}&i+j\leq N\\ 1&i+j>N\text{ and }i=N\\ 0&\text{ else,}\end{cases} (43)

and

W(i,j)→(i+1,j)={ii+ji+j≤N1i+j>N​ and ​i<N0 else,W_{(i,j)\to(i+1,j)}=\begin{cases}\frac{i}{i+j}&i+j\leq N\\ 1&i+j>N\text{ and }i<N\\ 0&\text{ else,}\end{cases} (44)

with all other edge weights equaling zero. Setting these edge weights creates a graph where all nodes in the bottom-right triangle have balanced inflow, i.e.,

Definition 3 (Balanced Inflow).

Let i+j=Li+j=L and consider the set of incoming paths to node (i,j)(i,j) as

𝒫(i,j)={(i1,j1),(i2,j2),…,(iL−1,jL−1),(iL,jL), where (i1,j1)=(1,1) and (iL,jL)=(i,j)}.\mathcal{P}(i,j)=\Big\{(i_{1},j_{1}),(i_{2},j_{2}),...,(i_{L-1},j_{L-1}),(i_{L},j_{L})\text{, where }(i_{1},j_{1})=(1,1)\text{ and }(i_{L},j_{L})=(i,j)\Big\}. (45)

A graph has balanced inflow if

∑{(ii′,ji′)}i′=1L∈𝒫⁡(i,j)∏l=1L−1W(il,jl)→(il+1,jl+1)=1L−1.\sum\limits_{\begin{subarray}{c}\{(i_{i^{\prime}},j_{i^{\prime}})\}_{i^{\prime}=1}^{L}\\ \in\mathcal{P}(i,j)\end{subarray}}\prod\limits_{l=1}^{L-1}W_{(i_{l},j_{l})\to(i_{l+1},j_{l+1})}=\frac{1}{L-1}. (46)

In English, this property encodes the idea of balanced inflow we discussed earlier—nodes that are equally far away from the root can all potentially receive the same error budget (although in practice, rejections in the lower-right triangle may thwart this effort). Proving that the Hamming SGT has balanced inflow is simple by induction on LL. This graph structure plays well with coordinatewise monotonicity and other such settings where the goal is to push from one corner to another in the space of hypotheses.

At a high level, the Hamming SGT improves on the fallback procedure when there are many rejections in the lower-right triangle. Indeed, the Hamming SGT is much more powerful in this region, since the error budget is more concentrated. In the best-case scenario, where all of the lower-right triangle is rejected, each node along the main diagonal gets a budget of δN−1\frac{\delta}{N-1}, and a fallback procedure is performed on the upper-left triangle. However, the graph’s structure can also hurt us; if a large fraction of nulls fail to be rejected in the lower-right triangle, the procedure could be less effective in rejecting an extreme setting of λ\lambda. Thus, we suggest the use of the Hamming SGT if there is reason to believe that the lower-right triangle will contain many rejections. We repeat that balanced inflow is not a necessary condition for a SGT graph to perform well, and in Section 6 we find that other approaches are more powerful.

Appendix E Alternative Approach: Uniform Concentration

Rather than use multiple testing, one can consider creating risk-controlling predictions using uniform concentration results. We outline this strategy below. Unfortunately, this approach is typically much more conservative than the multiple testing approach, even when using state-of-the-art concentration results. This is evidenced in our many simulations. Nonetheless, since this is a seemingly natural alternative, we record this approach in detail here.

E.1 Framework

We stated how uniform bounds lead to risk control in Proposition 8.

The main challenge is to come up with a valid uniform confidence bound R+R^{+}. We have developed such bounds, stating the technical details in Appendix E.2. In the experiments presented in the main text, we find that this is less powerful than the multiple-testing approach.

E.2 A new class of concentration inequalities for self-normalized empirical processes

We next develop a state-of-the art set of uniform concentration results for our setting. Recalling that

R^​(𝒯λ)=1n​∑i=1nL⁡(𝒯λ​(Xi),Yi),\hat{R}(\mathcal{T}_{\lambda})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}L(\mathcal{T}_{\lambda}(X_{i}),Y_{i}),

we can view {R^​(𝒯λ):λ∈Λ}\{\hat{R}(\mathcal{T}_{\lambda}):\lambda\in\Lambda\} as an empirical process indexed by λ\lambda. The simplest empirical process is the empirical CDF. The celebrated Dvoretzky-Kiefer-Wolfowitz-Massart (DKWM) inequality bounds the absolute difference |F^n​(w)−F​(w)||\hat{F}_{n}(w)-F(w)|. Although the constant is tight, the sup-difference metric ignores the non-constant variance of F^n​(w)\hat{F}_{n}(w). Specifically, n​F^n​(w)∼Binom⁡(n,F⁡(w))n\hat{F}_{n}(w)\sim\mathrm{Binom}(n,F(w)) and thus Var⁡[F^n​(w)]=F⁡(w)​(1−F⁡(w))/n\mathrm{Var}[\hat{F}_{n}(w)]=F(w)(1-F(w))/n. As a result, when F⁡(w)F(w) is close to 00 or 11, F^n​(w)\hat{F}_{n}(w) is more concentrated around F⁡(w)F(w).

To improve the DKWM bounds for tail events, a line of work has established concentration inequalities for self-normalized empirical processes [68, 72, 73, 74, 75]. In particular, they derived upper tail bounds for

supw∈ℝF^n​(w)−F​(w)F^n​(w)​ and ​supw∈ℝF​(w)−F^n​(w)F⁡(w),\sup_{w\in\mathbb{R}}\frac{\hat{F}_{n}(w)-F(w)}{\sqrt{\hat{F}_{n}(w)}}\text{ and }\sup_{w\in\mathbb{R}}\frac{F(w)-\hat{F}_{n}(w)}{\sqrt{F(w)}},

where F^n​(w)\hat{F}_{n}(w) denotes the empirical CDF of nn i.i.d. samples W1,…,WnW_{1},\ldots,W_{n} drawn from the distribution FF. For instance, [68] prove that, with probability 1−δ1-\delta,

supw∈ℝF​(w)−F^n​(w)F⁡(w)≤4n​log⁡(8​(n+1)α)=O⁡(log⁡nn).\sup_{w\in\mathbb{R}}\frac{F(w)-\hat{F}_{n}(w)}{\sqrt{F(w)}}\leq\sqrt{\frac{4}{n}\log\left(\frac{8(n+1)}{\alpha}\right)}=O\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{n}}\right).

When F^n​(w)=O⁡(log⁡n/n)\hat{F}_{n}(w)=O(\log n/n), the Anthony–Shaw-Taylor inequality yields an upper confidence bound of F⁡(w)F(w) of order O⁡(log⁡n/n)O(\log n/n) as well, while the DKWM inequality implies an upper confidence bound of F⁡(w)F(w) of order O⁡(1/n)O(1/\sqrt{n}). Thus the former yields a tighter results for rare events for large nn.

In our context, R^​(𝒯λ)\hat{R}(\mathcal{T}_{\lambda}) is more complicated than the empirical CDF because the summands are no longer binary. We adapt the proofs of [68], [69], and [76] to the general case and further improve their constants using the recently developed tools for sampling without replacement [77] and weighted sums of Rademacher variables [78, 79]. To state the general results, we consider a generic empirical process

s^n​(λ)=1n​∑i=1nS⁡(λ,Zi),s⁡(λ)=𝔼⁡[S⁡(λ,Zi)],S⁡(λ,Zi)∈[0,1]​ almost surely for every ​λ∈Λ.\hat{s}_{n}(\lambda)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}S(\lambda;Z_{i}),\quad s(\lambda)=\mathbb{E}[S(\lambda;Z_{i})],\quad S(\lambda;Z_{i})\in[0,1]\text{ almost surely for every }\lambda\in\Lambda. (47)

Note that S⁡(λ,Zi)=L⁡(Tλ​(Xi),Yi)S(\lambda;Z_{i})=L(T_{\lambda}(X_{i}),Y_{i}) in our context. Furthermore, we define Δ⁡(n)\Delta(n) as the

Δ⁡(n)=supz1,…,zn|{{S⁡(λ,z1),…,S⁡(λ,zn)}:λ∈Λ}|.\Delta(n)=\sup_{z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}}\bigg|\big\{\{S(\lambda;z_{1}),\ldots,S(\lambda;z_{n})\}:\lambda\in\Lambda\big\}\bigg|. (48)

In the literature, log⁡Δ⁡(n)\log\Delta(n) is often referred to as the growth function [80, Section 2].

Theorem E.1.

Under the setting (47), for any η≥0\eta\geq 0,

E.3 Uniform upper confidence bound for RCP

From these general results, we obtain the following corollary, which will result in a practical algorithm momentarily.

Corollary E.1.

Let

R+​(𝒯λ):=R^​(𝒯λ)+t⁡(η,δ)​R^​(𝒯λ)+η+t​(η,δ)24+t​(η,δ)22.R^{+}(\mathcal{T}_{\lambda}):=\hat{R}(\mathcal{T}_{\lambda})+t(\eta;\delta)\sqrt{\hat{R}(\mathcal{T}_{\lambda})+\eta+\frac{t(\eta;\delta)^{2}}{4}}+\frac{t(\eta;\delta)^{2}}{2}.

where t⁡(η,δ)t(\eta;\delta) is defined as the tt that solves

δ=infγ∈(0,1),n′∈ℤ+​min⁡{Δ⁡(n+n′)​exp⁡{−g2​(t,n,n′,γ,κ−)}1−exp⁡{−g1​(t,n′,γ,η)},Δ⁡(2​n)​g~​(n⁡(1+η)2​(1−γ)​t)1−exp⁡{−g1​(t,n,γ,η)}},\delta=\underset{\gamma\in(0,1),n^{\prime}\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}}{\inf}\min\left\{\frac{\Delta(n+n^{\prime})\exp\big\{-g_{2}(t;n,n^{\prime},\gamma,\kappa^{-})\big\}}{1-\exp\{-g_{1}(t;n^{\prime},\gamma,\eta)\}},\frac{\Delta(2n)\tilde{g}\left(\sqrt{\frac{n(1+\eta)}{2}}(1-\gamma)t\right)}{1-\exp\{-g_{1}(t;n,\gamma,\eta)\}}\right\},

where the functions and quantities are defined in Theorem E.1 and E.2. Then

ℙ⁡(R⁡(𝒯λ)≤R+​(𝒯λ)​ for all ​λ∈Λ)≥1−δ.\mathbb{P}(R(\mathcal{T}_{\lambda})\leq R^{+}(\mathcal{T}_{\lambda})\text{ for all }\lambda\in\Lambda)\geq 1-\delta.

An optimal choice of η\eta

The parameter η\eta needs to be chosen in advance. For a given level (α,δ)(\alpha,\delta), however, there is an optimal choice. Let

x⁡(η,δ):=α−t⁡(η,δ)​α+η,x(\eta;\delta):=\alpha-t(\eta;\delta)\sqrt{\alpha+\eta},

which is the largest solution xx of

α=x+t⁡(η,δ)​x+η+t​(η,δ)24+t​(η,δ)22.\alpha=x+t(\eta;\delta)\sqrt{x+\eta+\frac{t(\eta;\delta)^{2}}{4}}+\frac{t(\eta;\delta)^{2}}{2}.

This is the largest value for which FDP⁡(𝒯)≤x\mathrm{FDP}(\mathcal{T})\leq x implies that FDR+​(𝒯)≤α\mathrm{FDR}^{+}(\mathcal{T})\leq\alpha. In other words, with η\eta fixed, our procedure will find the largest λ\lambda such that FDP⁡(𝒯λ)≤x⁡(η,δ)\mathrm{FDP}(\mathcal{T}_{\lambda})\leq x(\eta;\delta), and select this value as λ^\hat{\lambda}. Thus, we should select the value of η\eta that makes x⁡(η,δ)x(\eta;\delta) as small as possible;

η∗​(δ):=arg⁡minη≥0​x​(η,δ)\eta^{*}(\delta):=\underset{\eta\geq 0}{\arg\min}\ x(\eta;\delta)

is the best value of η\eta.

E.4 Concrete instantiation for FDR control

To apply Corollary E.1 for FDR control, we need to derive the growth function. Let Zi=(Xi,Yi)Z_{i}=(X_{i},Y_{i}), {1,…,K}\{1,\ldots,K\} be the set of labels, and

Λi​j:=inf{λ∈ℝ:j∉𝒯λ​(Xi)}\Lambda_{ij}:=\inf\{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}:j\not\in\mathcal{T}_{\lambda}(X_{i})\}

In our example, 𝒯λ\mathcal{T}_{\lambda} is decreasing in λ\lambda. Thus,

FDR=𝔼⁡[S⁡(λ,Zi)],where ​S​(λ,Zi)=∑j=1mI⁡(Λi​j≤λ,j∉Yi)∑j=1mI⁡(Λi​j≤λ).\mathrm{FDR}=\mathbb{E}[S(\lambda;Z_{i})],\quad\text{where }S(\lambda;Z_{i})=\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{m}I(\Lambda_{ij}\leq\lambda,j\not\in Y_{i})}{\sum_{j=1}^{m}I(\Lambda_{ij}\leq\lambda)}.

Here, 0/00/0 is defined as 00. Note that (S⁡(λ,Z1),…,S⁡(λ,Zn))(S(\lambda;Z_{1}),\ldots,S(\lambda;Z_{n})) changes value only when λ=Λi​j\lambda=\Lambda_{ij} for some ii and jj, and thus

Δ⁡(n)≤n​m+1.\Delta(n)\leq nm+1. (53)

In Algorithm 3 below, we present the full algorithm corresponding to Corollary 8, specialized to the FDR control setting from Section 3 for concreteness. In addition, in Figure 13, we report numerical information about the size of the bound. In particular, we show the empirical FDR that must be achieved in order to conclude that the true FDR is below α\alpha with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta; that is, x⁡(η∗,δ)x(\eta^{*};\delta) in our notation above. When this curve is farther below the nominal rate α\alpha, it means that the procedure is quite conservative. We find that the procedure is heavily conservative until nn is of order 10510^{5}. This provides further evidence that the uniform concentration approach is looser than the multiple testing approach, so it requires a much larger amount of calibration data.

We prove (52) first. We will use the same notation hereafter as in the proof of Theorem E.1. By (63) and (67) with n′=nn^{\prime}=n, it remains to prove that
